questions.title: A tariff on an imported staple
questions.stem:
Lumen is a small price-taking economy. With free trade, grain costs 12 dinars per sack. Domestic demand Qd = 200 − 5P and supply Qs = 20 + 5P, measured in thousands of sacks each month. Traders can import freely at the given world price. Assume competitive markets and no transport costs or externalities for the calculations.

The farm ministry proposes a tariff of 3 dinars per sack. Farmers say volatile earnings discourage investment. In the poorest fifth of households grain accounts for 18% of expenditure; in the richest fifth it accounts for 3%. A trial of crop storage reduced post-harvest losses but requires reliable electricity. The government can alternatively fund time-limited income support for small farmers from general taxation.

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the free-trade quantities supplied and demanded domestically.

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.prompt: Calculate monthly spending on grain imports under free trade.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Calculate the level of imports after the tariff and the resulting monthly tariff revenue.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the loss of consumer surplus per month caused by the tariff.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: Calculate the gain in domestic producer surplus per month.

parts.label: a(vi)
parts.prompt: Calculate the change in national welfare per month. Explain why counting only tariff revenue gives a misleading result.

parts.label: a(vii)
parts.prompt: Using a tariff diagram, distinguish the part of the efficiency loss due to excess domestic production from that due to reduced consumption.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the information and your knowledge of economics, recommend a policy to support vulnerable grain farmers while protecting access to food in Lumen.

steps.text: Qs = 20 + 5 × 12 = 80 thousand sacks (1). Qd = 200 − 5 × 12 = 140 thousand sacks per month (1).
Imports = 140 − 80 = 60 thousand sacks (1). Spending = 60,000 × 12 = 720,000 dinars (1).
The domestic price rises to 15, giving Qd = 125 and Qs = 95 thousand (1). Imports = 30 thousand (1). Revenue = 30,000 × 3 = 90,000 dinars per month (1).
Use the area between the two price lines and below demand (1). With linear demand, average quantity = (140 + 125)/2 = 132.5 thousand (1). Loss = 3 × 132.5 thousand = 397,500 dinars (1).
Average domestic supply over the price rise = (80 + 95)/2 thousand (1). Gain = 3 × 87,500 = 262,500 dinars (1).

Change = producer gain + revenue − consumer loss (1) = 262,500 + 90,000 − 397,500 = −45,000 dinars (1). Revenue is a transfer from buyers to the government (1). Extra high-cost domestic production and lost consumption account for the efficiency loss (1).

Draw domestic demand and supply, with horizontal world-price and tariff-inclusive price lines. Mark the four quantities and the separate triangular areas (up to 2). Production loss = ½ × 3 × 15,000 = 22,500 dinars where domestic marginal cost exceeds world cost. Consumption loss = 22,500 where willingness to pay exceeds the world cost but purchases cease (up to 2).

Use time-limited, means-tested farmer income support rather than raising the market grain price. The tariff transfers 262,500 dinars monthly to domestic producers but costs consumers 397,500 and creates a 45,000 efficiency loss. With grain taking 18% of the poorest households' budgets, a price rise can be especially burdensome. An income payment need not increase the marginal reward for uneconomic output.

Targeting requires credible farm income records, general taxation has opportunity costs and large farmers may capture payments. Income relief does little for productivity. Storage support could help where losses are large but its value depends on reliable electricity. Set an expiry and monitor farm income, retail food prices and take-up by small farmers. Credit a defended tariff or storage recommendation that deals with these costs.

Best fit, 0–10. 0: no relevant response. 1–2: a policy is named with minimal reasoning. 3–4: a plausible policy with partial explanation. 5–6: a relevant mechanism and some use of the case, with limited trade-offs. 7–8: developed theory, relevant data and reasoned consideration of limitations. 9–10: a well-supported, feasible recommendation synthesising case evidence, economic reasoning and the most consequential trade-offs. Credit a different justified recommendation.

questions.title: A currency under pressure
questions.stem:
Meridia's central bank maintains a managed exchange rate. The rate begins at 5 local units per US dollar; maintaining the announced rate requires sales of foreign reserves when demand for dollars rises. Fuel and medicine are imported under short contracts. Some exporters can increase shipments after a year, but transport capacity is currently tight. Local firms service unhedged dollar loans from local-currency revenues.

A possible new rate is 6 local units per US dollar. All flows in the table are annual US-dollar billions. Ignore valuation changes and errors for the flow calculation. Treat net private financing as the only non-reserve funding for the current-account balance. Beginning reserves are US$6 billion. Annual imports of goods and services used in the reserve-cover calculation are US$12 billion.

| Current-account item | Receipts | Payments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goods | 8.0 | 10.0 |
| Services | 3.0 | 2.0 |
| Primary income | 0.4 | 1.3 |
| Secondary income | 0.7 | 0.4 |

parts.label: a(i)
parts.prompt: Calculate the goods balance and the services balance.

parts.label: a(iii)
parts.prompt: Net private financing supplies US$1.0 billion. Calculate reserve use, ending reserves and months of import cover.

parts.label: a(iv)
parts.prompt: Calculate the percentage rise in the local-currency price of a US dollar and the percentage fall in the dollar value of a local unit if the new rate is adopted.

parts.label: a(v)
parts.prompt: A firm owes US$4 million due immediately. Calculate the change in the local-currency value of this liability at the new rate.

parts.label: a(vi)
parts.prompt: Using a foreign exchange diagram for US dollars, explain how intervention can maintain the initial exchange rate when demand for dollars rises.

parts.label: a(vii)
parts.prompt: Explain why lowering the value of the local currency might initially widen the trade deficit measured in local currency.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Using the information and your knowledge of economics, recommend an exchange-rate policy for Meridia in response to the continuing demand for dollars.

steps.text: Goods = 8 − 10 = −US$2 billion (1). Services = 3 − 2 = +US$1 billion (1).
Net primary income = −0.9 and net secondary income = +0.3 billion. Combine with net goods and services of −1 (1). Balance = −US$1.6 billion (1).
Reserve use = 1.6 − 1.0 = US$0.6 billion (1). Ending reserves = 6 − 0.6 = US$5.4 billion (1). Monthly imports = 12/12 = US$1 billion, giving 5.4 months of cover (1).
The dollar rises from 5 to 6, an increase of 1/5 × 100 = 20% (1). One local unit changes from US$0.20 to US$1/6 (1). Its dollar value falls by 16.67% (1). The two denominators differ.
The liability rises from 5 × 4 = 20 million to 6 × 4 = 24 million local units (1). Increase = 4 million local units (1).

Label local units per US dollar and quantity of dollars. Shift dollar demand right and show the excess demand at the original rate (up to 2). The central bank sells dollars for local currency to fill the gap, maintaining the rate while drawing down finite reserves (up to 2).

With import volumes fixed by contracts, each dollar of imports costs more local currency. If export prices are fixed in local currency and capacity limits additional sales, local export receipts initially rise less than import expenditure. The later outcome depends on demand responses, capacity and currency of invoicing. The quotation alone does not determine the trade balance.

Allow a phased adjustment with limited intervention against abrupt movements. The annual funding gap of US$0.6 billion reduces cover from six to 5.4 months. Repeated defence without new financing would erode the buffer for essential imports. A weaker currency can curb imports and support exports over time.

Immediate repricing raises the domestic cost of the illustrative dollar loan by 4 million local units; essential import demand is relatively inelastic. With tight transport capacity, rapid export expansion is unlikely. Aggressive defence avoids the immediate shock but can invite larger reserve losses if the rate is unsustainable. Publish conditions for intervention and monitor cover, debt service and essential prices. A temporary defence is defensible if the pressure is transient and financing is credible.

Best fit, 0–10. 0: no relevant response. 1–2: a policy is named with minimal reasoning. 3–4: a plausible policy with partial explanation. 5–6: a relevant mechanism and some use of the case, with limited trade-offs. 7–8: developed theory, relevant data and reasoned consideration of limitations. 9–10: a well-supported, feasible recommendation synthesising case evidence, economic reasoning and the most consequential trade-offs. Credit a different justified recommendation.
